name: Emeka Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What does a usual day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I check the van's tools and the job sheets at the yard, then we drive to whichever line needs attention. I'm still junior, so I watch the senior worker's hands closely; I like solving a fault, but the reports after a long shift can be harder than the repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that the little AI help on our reports is all right if we still check every line ourselves. I used it once to tidy a note after a storm call, but it made the damaged crossarm sound like a routine inspection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our hands are needed and the company has more repair requests than crews this season, so I don't see my job going from a bit of software. Still, our mortgage payment lands before my partner's clinic pay some months, and two children can turn a comfortable week into a tight one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my line shifts and continue showing the foreman the original field notes beside any AI-cleaned report. In the first year I'd set aside 40 from each payday for the mortgage buffer, provided the clinic hours hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be mostly at ease about the work itself. The money still keeps me attentive; I know one missed clinic shift can eat the spare 40.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep the rough notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring I wrote that the top crossarm was split, and the polished version dropped the word split. The foreman caught it before anyone planned the wrong repair, which is why I keep the dirty notebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How steady are your partner's hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner is a clinic receptionist with regular hours most weeks, but the clinic cancels shifts when the doctor is away. We have about four months of expenses saved, and I'd like a little more.

say: I would accept **minor report help** if the crew checks the facts.
I would keep the **original field notes** beside polished software text.
think: I expect **repair demand** to sustain my line shifts in this picture.
Our mortgage and variable **clinic hours** still make the budget worth watching.
do: Keep taking **line shifts** and show the foreman original notes.
Set aside **40 per payday** if clinic hours remain steady.
feel: Mostly **at ease** about work, with a watchful eye on money.
S0.quote: The foreman caught it before anyone planned the wrong repair, which is why I keep the dirty notebook.
fieldNote: He has tried AI in a limited way and noticed a **lost safety detail** in its polished report.
His roughly **four-month cushion** eases worry, while mortgage timing and clinic shifts still matter.

steps.text: Keep taking line shifts and show original notes to the foreman
Set aside 40 each payday if clinic hours hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office will feel this first: software can write outage messages and move appointments, but somebody still needs to know which feeder is actually down. Our union ought to get the dispatchers and crews in the same room before a new system sets the roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can imagine fewer call handlers and a smaller planning team, which might leave us with more work packed into each shift. Robots come more slowly, but my place as a junior worker isn't fixed if the company decides it can send leaner crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd sit with Noor, the dispatcher, for a shift to learn how faults get prioritised and raise roster questions at the union branch. If the new system arrives, I'd practise the approved fault-mapping tool with a senior crew member and apply to another utility yard if my paid hours drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm curious enough to try a tool once someone I trust has checked it. I'm also uneasy about Noor having to train software that could take away her desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask Noor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask why she put the hospital feeder ahead of a row of shops during the last outage, because the screen doesn't show her whole reasoning. I want to know what our crew should challenge when an automated job ticket looks wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why learn a tool you distrust?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've used a report helper on small jobs and found a mistake, so I know how to check rather than just agree. A mapping tool might save a drive, but I'd use it only after the company signs it off for live work.

say: I would bring **dispatchers and crews** together before software sets the roster.
I would remind colleagues that **fault priority** needs local judgment.
think: I expect office posts to shrink and **crew shifts** to become more crowded.
My junior position could lose hours despite slower **robot adoption**.
do: Shadow Noor for a shift and raise **roster questions** at the union branch.
Practise the approved **fault-mapping tool** with a senior worker.
Apply to another **utility yard** if paid hours fall.
feel: Curious about checked tools and **uneasy** for dispatch staff.
S1.quote: I want to know what our crew should challenge when an automated job ticket looks wrong.
fieldNote: He learns from a **named dispatcher** and treats her judgment as useful field knowledge.
He is willing to test a **signed-off tool**, while linking job applications to actual lost hours.

steps.text: Raise roster questions at the union branch after shadowing Noor

Apply to another utility yard if paid hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the yard that full thinking AI by 2028 would change dispatch, buying and fault plans before a robot can climb beside us. I would want the union to see the company's numbers on crews, not just the software demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 45 in 2028, with the children still in school and a mortgage to pay. Around 2031, when robots can do the physical repair, a junior like me could be easier to replace than the people who know every old line by sight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the branch rep for the crew plan now and stop the weekend takeaway so the buffer lasts longer. In 2029 I'd keep taking field shifts, use the approved map to check job tickets against the old diagrams, and submit an application to the water network if our roster loses days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can think through those steps, but I'm frightened of getting the timing wrong. Four months of expenses is useful for a gap, not for years of mortgage payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your children notice first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd notice the takeaway gone before they understood an automated dispatch plan. I'd explain that I still have work this year, but we're putting more aside because the next three years are uncertain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the water network really be safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know; it has pumps and pipes that robots might handle later too. I'd apply only if there were paid openings and our line hours fell, and I'd ask about the work before handing in notice.

say: I would tell the yard that **2028 thinking AI** reaches office tasks first.
I would ask the union for **crew numbers** before believing a software demonstration.
think: I will be **45 in 2028**, with school-age children and a mortgage.
I fear **2031 repair robots** may put junior lineworkers first in line for cuts.
do: Ask for the **crew plan** and cancel weekend takeaway now.
Keep **field shifts** in 2029 and check automated tickets.
Apply to the **water network** if our roster loses days.
feel: Frightened of mistiming a move despite a **four-month buffer**.
S2.quote: Four months of expenses is useful for a gap, not for years of mortgage payments.
fieldNote: His **2029 plan** keeps paid field work while using approved maps to challenge job tickets.
He understands the water network may face later **robot exposure** and would seek an actual opening first.

steps.text: Ask the union branch for the company crew plan
Cancel the family weekend takeaway now
Keep field shifts and check job tickets against diagrams in 2029
Apply to paid water network openings if line days fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives workers a chance to test the new tools properly and press for paid training. Dispatch changes by 2031, and we should know which duties remain before repair robots become capable around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 48 when the thinking work changes and 51 at the robot date, and neither age puts me close to a retirement I can afford. The children will be older, but the mortgage won't disappear just because they leave school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'd ask the training officer which line-inspection certificate the utility accepts and put 40 per payday into savings when clinic hours allow. If the employer funds the course, I'd enrol; in 2032 I'd keep paid field work and apply for an inspection opening once I had the certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more able to act with five years than with two. I still worry that the course could lead to a queue of lineworkers chasing the same small set of inspection posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes the certificate useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An inspector has to notice heat damage and a bad bond, and I need supervised practice before I'd sign anything. I would ask to see where recent graduates actually went, rather than trusting a course advert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be learning while still doing line work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if the utility pays for the training time; I can't stop earning and leave my partner to carry the mortgage. I'd move to inspection only for a real paid vacancy.

say: I would ask for **tested tools** and paid training during the warning years.
I would tell colleagues the **2031 and 2034** changes need separate plans.
think: I will be **48 then 51**, with no affordable retirement in sight.
Older children do not erase our **mortgage**, and inspection openings may be scarce.
do: Ask which **inspection certificate** the utility accepts.
Save **40 per payday** when clinic hours allow.
Enrol if funded and apply for **inspection work** after qualifying.
feel: More able to act, while wary of a **crowded job queue**.
S3.quote: I'd move to inspection only for a real paid vacancy.
fieldNote: He checks both the **accepted certificate** and actual graduate destinations before committing to study.
His plan depends on **paid training time** and continued line wages through the 2032 transition.

steps.text: Save 40 each payday when clinic hours allow
Enrol in the accepted inspection certificate if the utility funds it
Keep taking paid line shifts in 2032
Apply for a paid inspection vacancy after qualifying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company has a decade to bring the union into equipment trials and explain where people will work afterward. I'd volunteer to test a safe, approved mapping tool now, but I wouldn't sign off a live repair from a screen alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036 I may have more experience than I do now, and at 56 in 2039 the robots could still take the climbing work. My children will be grown or nearly grown, but I'd need to check what our savings and benefits really amount to before saying I can retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the line job, try approved mapping with a senior worker, and ask for the utility's funded inspection course when places open. In 2037 I'd apply for paid inspection work if qualified, and keep building our mortgage buffer until a new contract was signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the first picture where I can imagine a gradual handover rather than a scramble. It isn't a promise: a decade can still end with me needing a wage and no vacant inspection post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from an equipment trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want lineworkers to record every time a map missed an old spur or sent us to the wrong isolation point. A trial has to leave a paper trail the union can question, not just a glossy success rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you plan to stop working at 56?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can't say that without seeing my actual pension record and the mortgage balance then. I would rather have a signed job in inspection than hope a retirement number works out.

say: I would seek **union oversight** of equipment trials during the decade.
I would test approved maps but keep **human sign-off** on live repairs.
think: I will be **53 in 2036** and 56 when repair robots arrive.
I need a real **pension record** and mortgage balance before considering retirement.
do: Keep the **line job** and test mapping with a senior worker.
Take a **funded inspection course** if places open.
Apply for paid **inspection work** in 2037 if qualified.
feel: Able to picture a handover, but wary of **empty vacancies**.
S4.quote: I would rather have a signed job in inspection than hope a retirement number works out.
fieldNote: He imagines **union-reviewed trials** with a record of mapping misses, grounded in his past report error.
Even with ten years, he plans for **paid employment**, not an assumed pension or settled children.

steps.text: Test approved mapping with a senior lineworker
Keep taking paid line shifts during training
Take the utility inspection course if a funded place opens
Apply for paid inspection openings in 2037 if qualified

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most; the office changes quickly and we get only a few years before repair robots. I'd need the crew plan in writing, paid time to train, and a way for workers to challenge unsafe job tickets.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns a wrong instruction when a computer draws the route. I want a named person who listens when a lineworker says the diagram is wrong, because the line won't care whose software made it.

headlineQuote: I want a named person who listens when a lineworker says the diagram is wrong, because the line won't care whose software made it.
portrait: Emeka is a **43-year-old junior lineworker** with two school-age children, a partner and a mortgage.
He sometimes uses **AI report help**, but checks it against his field notebook after it missed a damaged crossarm.
His household has about **four months** of expenses saved, while his partner’s clinic shifts can vary.
He seeks **tested tools**, union scrutiny and paid inspection training while preserving line wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because office changes come quickly and repair robots follow around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a written **crew plan**, paid training time and a way to challenge unsafe job tickets.
